newsitem.title: UK: Uranium price boom seen as stocks dwindle.
newsitem.headline: Uranium price boom seen as stocks dwindle.

text.p: After two decades of decline, uranium production and exploration have come back into fashion since prices began a sharp recovery last year, a Uranium Institute conference heard on Friday.
But delegates said prices will have to rise further to encourage producers to meet rising nuclear generation demand.

World uranium prices have almost doubled in the last two years to $16 per pound, but new production still only represents about 55 percent of demand -- almost half of today's 61,400 tonnes annual demand is met by the world's huge stockpiles, accumulated largely as a result of the 1970s arms race -- but these are at last diminshing.
Uranium Institute analysts now believe that there are only 80,000 tonnes of excess stocks left, equivalent to just over one year of current world demand.
"Even with continuing disposals of excess material held by governments, additional mine production will be needed," said Phillip Crowson, an economist at mining giant RTZ Corp.
The Uranium Institute said current plans to expand uranium production will still fall short by 5,000 tonnes per annum from 2000 to 2015, under its reference case scenario.

"Uranium reserves are clearly sufficient, but the development of known deposits to create additional capacity is only likely to occur if sufficient financial incentive is available," said Horst Keese, a senior advisor to Germany's Nukem, presenting the Institute's market report.

Some of the forecast demand rise would be met by blending down Russia's huge stocks of weapons-grade uranium, Keese said. This would rise to a plateau of about 5,000 tonnes of uranium per year between 2007 and 2015.
Also fuel reprocessing would create a modest extra supply.
"Even with these, there is still likely to be a substantial supply gap, which will need to be filled," he added.
There were already firm plans for new production in Austalia, Canada and the United States, but producers said only higher prices would create sufficient incentive to meet demand.
"It appears that recently prevailing prices are still insufficient to support significant new exploration," Georges Capus, senior market analyst at French nuclear giant Cogema, told the conference.

Uranium Institute analysts were reluctant to make any price forecasts, for fear of contravening cartel regulations, but delegates at the conference said prices would have to rise "substantially" over the next five years.

Even substantial price rises will have little impact on the economics of nuclear power generation, however, because fuel costs constitute less than two percent of total costs, according to Ingemar Lindholm, director of Sweden's SKB nuclear generator.
